text: So they aimed it into the atmosphere, where it'd burn up before it could smack a moon. After thirteen years sniffing around Saturn's moons, the last thing you wanted was drifting debris or Earth bacteria landing on Enceladus, where plumes keep spewing water and organics. It's exactly where you'd look for interesting chemistry or microbes, so the team didn't want junk dropped there. Enceladus plumes are full of the stuff you'd want to sample, so even a little Cassini residue would be a pain to explain later. With fuel low at mission end, atmospheric entry was the clean way to retire it.

Your stationary leg is doing more than standing still. When you push off, the foot you plant takes your whole body weight plus the force of the push, and it has to be completely stable so you don't lose balance while the other foot is on the board. If the board is tilted or your stance is off, that planted leg gets squeezed between the ground and your center of mass, and after a while the muscles, joints and tendons start to complain.

Pain can point to a few things, and which one applies to you depends on where it hurts. If it's mostly around the knee, you're likely putting too much forward lean on it. Knees don't like staying locked under load like that for long. If it's the hip or groin area, you may be pushing too hard from the hip and not enough through the legs. That forces the hip flexors and adductors to do a lot of work with the leg fixed to the ground. If the pain is at the foot, arch or heel, your push foot may be absorbing impacts you're not used to, especially on rough pavement.

A practical way to check is to try a gentler ride and pay attention to how you're balancing. Stand tall on the board, keep your weight centered, and make smaller, smoother pushes. If the pain fades with that, it's mostly a technique issue. Also look at your setup: if the trucks are really loose or the board is flexing too much, your stationary leg has to overcorrect to keep the board stable, which adds load to it. Tightening trucks or using a stiffer board can help if that's the cause.

Don't just keep pushing through the pain. Skateboard injuries to the leg are usually from overuse or bad form rather than a single crash. If it hurts in the same spot every ride and gets worse the more you push, give it a few days, do light calf and hamstring stretches, and build back up slowly. If the pain is sharp, swelling or a specific pinching sensation, that's worth a physio check rather than guessing.

The term African American is a historical marker for descent, acting as a bridge to the ancestral homeland rather than a travel log or a passport. Most US black people are descendants of enslaved Africans brought over during the transatlantic slave trade, mostly from West and Central Africa, but the vast majority of those people haven't set foot on the continent themselves. It is the same idea as calling someone an Irish-American just because their great-grandparents emigrated from County Cork, or a German-American because their family left Bavaria. The Afro part is a shorthand for the continental roots, acknowledging those ancestral ties even when the current generation mostly knows Africa from books, family stories, or maybe a heritage trip. You don't have to have actually lived there to trace your lineage back to a specific region. For most of these families, the connection is deeply personal, like remembering a specific village name from West Africa that an older relative kept mentioning around the dinner table, a little anchor to a place they might never physically visit. The label tracks the lineage, not the current country of residence.

They mostly come in through informal routes: private traders, border crossings and black markets, plus whatever remains of state arsenals. People still get them because carrying a gun became the local norm during the war, so a lot of households kept rifles or pistols afterwards for protection against neighbours or militias. There's also a political reason, since small arms let local strongmen hold on to power and collect protection money, so they keep supplying their own side.

The twist is that the adverse effects aren't really what make drugs dangerous, because even a perfectly harmless drug would still hook you in other ways. You can take the side effects off the table and you still get the same problem, and that's the core thing that surprises people. When I think about it, the issue is the reward signal in your brain, and if a drug makes that signal huge, your body starts treating that specific high as the baseline of what's worth having. So you don't just stop because it stopped giving pleasure, you chase it because your baseline has moved.

Think about an actual scenario. Someone takes heroin, gets that intense euphoria, feels amazing, and then their brain is recording that this is the thing that matters now. The next time they do it, the first hit doesn't feel as good, so they need more to get the same result. That's the trap, and it works even if the drug doesn't damage your liver or make you sick. The damage isn't from a chemical wrecking your organs, it's from your brain deciding that a regular, moderate reward is no reward at all. That's why even a drug with zero adverse effects would still produce compulsive use, because the desire for more is a feature of how the pleasure circuitry works, not a defect. People notice this in everyday life too: the person who can't stop eating, who keeps drinking coffee, who goes back to the casino even when they're losing, isn't doing it because food or alcohol or cards are bad in a medical sense, it's because the brain is chasing the last hit of pleasure it remembers. That pattern is the real danger, and drugs with intense euphoria supercharge it.

There's also the social side. If a drug gives you intense pleasure and causes no adverse effects, you're not dealing with a medical problem, you're dealing with the same habit-forming pressure that gets people back to the thing. The question isn't whether the drug is chemically harmful, it's whether the pleasure is strong enough to reshape what feels normal, and the answer is that it can be. That's why you can't design a drug that gives you intense euphoria with zero adverse effects and expect people to stop using it. The absence of side effects doesn't remove the pull.

What keeps tripping up most people is thinking the problem is the drug itself. But when you actually look at how people behave, the compulsive chasing is the mechanism, and it happens even when the drug is harmless. That's the plain practical answer, and it's why the whole "zero adverse effects" idea doesn't solve the real issue.

Hi,
Your brother was just messing with your attention span, but the milk answer is your brain taking the path of least resistance. Cows and milk are so tightly bound in our heads that when you think about cows, the producer side of it just takes over. You weren't thinking about what they actually consume, you just grabbed the most obvious association. It's a classic semantic slip. You were focused on the milk the cow produces instead of the water it actually drinks. People make this mistake all the time, mostly because milk is literally the first word that pops into your head when you hear the word cow. The silk spelling was just a little test to see if you were focused, and the cow question was another twist to catch you zoning out. We do this sort of thing constantly. Next time just say water and see if he gives you that smug look.
Best,
Me

Hi,

You list a few house-buying questions but they don't come through in your email, so I'll just talk about the bits I care about most, and you can pick out whatever you actually need.

Start with a survey and an electrical check before you make an offer. I saw a guy walk into a place with peeling paint and no radon mention, then discover in the inspection that the wiring was old, and that cost him a week in negotiation. A loan pre-approval letter helps too. Sellers can tell who's serious, and it's not the same as final loan approval, but it gets you a better look.

If rates move while you're searching, don't lock early unless you're ready to close. You can usually hold for 10 to 30 days, but if the purchase is off schedule, the lock can expire. I'd only lock when you're about a week from closing.

And don't skip the nighttime neighborhood walk. You can see who's out, how the streets feel, whether cars are parked weird, or if the place goes dark after ten. That information matters more than a glossy listing photo.

Send me the specific questions when you can, I'll answer those properly.

Best,
Alex

The main difference is that a 3-in-1 is one compromise formula, not three products in one bottle. It has to clean hair, skin, and scalp at once, so it can't push hard on any single job. Think of the 3-in-1 as a universal cleanser. The formulation is balanced, not optimized. Separate shampoo targets the scalp, separate conditioner targets the cuticle, separate bodywash targets skin. The 3-in-1 has to please all three, so the surfactant and conditioning sets get diluted.

Compared with regular shampoo, a 3-in-1 usually cleans more gently. That can be good for sensitive skin, but less effective at stripping oil or product buildup. In a tiny travel shower, it saves carrying three bottles. The 2-in-1 is already a split personality: hair first, conditioning second, and it usually has more detangling agents. The 3-in-1 adds body-skin considerations, so you'd expect more moisturizers and a milder detergent load.

In practice, if you have thick or very oily hair, a dedicated shampoo does more. If your scalp gets dry, or you use a lot of styling product, separate conditioner still works better. The 3-in-1 is a convenience trade. Easier routine, acceptable results, but you lose some targeted benefit.

Hope that clears it up.

Cheers,

Yeah, they measure it right now with GPS. You can track a specific point on the ground, like a survey marker near the San Andreas fault, and see it shift a few centimeters over a year. Beyond guessing from old rocks, we have satellites tracking the physical movement of the crust in real time.

If you look at the Pacific and North American plates, they slide past each other, and the GPS data shows the exact speed. It’s surprisingly slow in human terms, maybe two centimeters a year, but over millions of years that distance adds up fast. You don't have to rely on fossils or the magnetic stripes on the ocean floor to get the current speed. The satellites make the whole thing verifiable. You can pull the data and see the coordinates shifting, it’s one of those things that sounds abstract until you actually look at the numbers. The tectonic shifts are constant, so the GPS coordinates never stop updating. It’s a pretty solid way to prove plate tectonics is actually happening.

For context, the North American plate is drifting westward at roughly two centimeters per year. It’s the kind of scale that’s hard to picture when you're just standing on the ground.

Let me know if you want me to walk through the magnetic evidence too.

Best,
Sam

Inbreeding doesn't lower IQ because relatives are "bad"; it mainly increases the odds that harmful recessive variants pair up in a child. A lot of cognitive ability runs in families, but the important bit here is recessive genetic load: many people carry small harmful variants without showing symptoms, because one copy isn't enough. When two closely related parents have a child, they're more likely to share those hidden variants, so the child can end up with two copies at once. In a family tree with little outside blood, this probability climbs with every generation of intermarriage.

That extra recessive load, combined with the general loss of genetic variety that comes with mating between relatives, can show up as weaker development, more vulnerability to illness, and lower average cognitive scores. It's not a fixed number for every child, and environment matters too, but the genetic mechanism is real.

The main reason is that the arm is built with thick muscle, tendons and bone layers, so it acts as a shock absorber. When a bullet or blade enters the arm, it has to punch through a lot of soft tissue before hitting the bone, and that resistance spreads out the force. That's different from the torso, where the muscles are much thinner and the heart, lungs, liver or spine sit close to the surface; a wound there hits important organs faster, which is why it usually feels more severe and dangerous.

In practice, even a shallow cut to the forearm feels less shocking than a similar wound to the chest or abdomen, because the limb has more padding and the threat to life is lower. There is also a psychological element; a limb wound is usually seen as easier to manage and less fatal, which changes how people experience the pain.

The short, direct answer: CO sticks to hemoglobin so tightly that it blocks oxygen, not because you're breathing the wrong gas in the usual way. Your red blood cells carry oxygen with hemoglobin, and carbon monoxide binds to that protein about twenty times more strongly than oxygen does, so once it's on there, oxygen can't take its place easily. That means your blood keeps circulating, but it's mostly carrying CO, not O2, and your tissues start starving.

Carbon dioxide in normal exposure isn't doing that to your oxygen transport. Your lungs and blood handle CO2 as a routine gas: you exhale it out, and it stays in the normal breathing cycle. It's only when it piles up that you get symptoms, and that's a different, much higher threshold situation. The poison in CO comes from that tight hemoglobin grab, which is why even fairly low concentrations cause headaches and dizziness. In other words, CO is the gas that quietly takes over the oxygen slots in your blood.

A practical picture: CO is produced when fuel burns without enough air, like a gas heater left on a low setting, or a car idling in a garage with the door closed. You don't smell or see it, which is the catch, and it's why you might feel "just a bit off" and put it down to tiredness until it's too late. That's why we run CO alarms, and why the alarm test button exists. CO2 alarms measure something else, like air that's getting stuffy and stale, not oxygen being stolen from your blood. The wiki point for new colleagues: if you hear a CO alarm, get to fresh air, check the heater or engine, and don't go back in until someone has found the source.

The brace is the position you assume when an impact seems likely, and it protects you by turning your body into a compact stable shape rather than letting it go loose in your seat. When a plane hits the ground hard, your body keeps moving until something stops it, and that sudden stop is what causes injuries. In the position you bend forward, tuck your head toward your knees, and grip your own shoulders or knees. That tuck stops your head from snapping forward and reduces neck strain.

It also keeps you from slapping into the seat, floor, or nearby people, and it helps you stay conscious so you can move if needed after impact. The compact shape helps with air flow by keeping your airway from being crushed, and it keeps the force spread over more of your body. You also stay in your seat, which matters when a crash throws people out of it.

To picture it, imagine crouching on a bus that swerves: you lower your center of gravity and keep your head down. On an aircraft, the crew will call for a brace, and you tuck into that same shape before impact. The practical benefit is that you get hit less, and you are more likely to get up or crawl out.

The reason most pre-industrial companies aren't familiar today is that they either didn't last, or they were absorbed into newer businesses. Many old shops and guild houses vanished during wars, financial crashes, and simple wear, and a company that still uses its founder's name doesn't necessarily have the same owners. So a brand's long history isn't the same as being a direct descendant of that person's business. When older firms survive, they usually get acquired, merged, or rebranded, and the original name drops out of public memory even if part of the business continues. That's why the household names people recognize are almost all from the industrial era.

The question sounds like it wants me to pick a side, so I’ll: if you get the same interest rate from both, the bank is usually the cheaper financing deal, not the dealership. The dealer’s lower advertised rate is real, but it often comes wrapped in extra costs. The bank doesn’t try to sell you add-ons.

Let’s make this concrete. Say you’re buying a $20,000 car with $3,000 down and borrowing $17,000. The bank offers 6% APR on a 60-month loan. Your monthly payment would be around $335, and the total interest paid over the term is roughly $3,100. The dealer offers 5.5% APR, which on its face looks better and saves you about $260 in interest. But then the dealer adds a document fee of $400, an extended service contract for $1,500, a roadside assistance package for $600, and GAP coverage for $800. Suddenly the “cheaper” dealer financing is costing you $2,300 in extras, which wipes out the interest savings.

I’ve learned this the hard way. At the dealer, the sales rep talked about the “special 5.5% rate” and made it sound like a bargain. I didn’t ask enough questions, and the extras were presented as convenient options. On my end, I took the bank’s offer and paid $250 in closing costs. The bank’s higher rate was offset by the absence of the dealer’s add-ons, and the total was lower. That’s the thing people miss: the lower rate isn’t the whole deal.

The dealer’s pricing is also more variable. Sometimes the “low rate” is a holdback or contingency, meaning it only applies for a limited window, or only if you take their financing. The bank’s rate, while higher, is straightforward. I don’t say the dealer’s loan is always worse, but when comparing apples to apples, the bank wins on total cost most of the time.

The bottom line for me is that financing cost isn’t just interest rate. If a dealer’s lower rate comes with add-ons that the bank doesn’t charge, the dealer’s deal can cost more overall. When I stopped looking only at the percentage and started looking at total out-of-pocket, the bank made more sense. That’s why, in many cases, financing through a bank is cheaper even though the dealership advertises a lower rate.

A friend of mine just told me he drives every morning on a 10 mile commute, and he's pretty sure at least one car in front of him reeks of weed. That's why I don't care how many states have legalized it, because the patchwork rules leave everyone else guessing who's sober and who isn't. In California I can smell smoke outside my window, while in Alabama that same behavior would still mean trouble. I've spent weeks learning the states where driving with a detectable THC level can actually get you a ticket, and the difference between the penalties has been eye opening. The patchwork means a driver can be legal at one state line and illegal at the next. To me that's a mess that needs a federal standard on what "impaired" actually means on the road, otherwise we're just trusting the nose test.

I keep coming back to the sodium-potassium pump, because it's the little machine that makes our electrical system tick. Every cell pushes more sodium out and more potassium in than it should, and that imbalance leaves cells sitting around minus seventy millivolts. When a nerve wants to fire it opens its sodium channels, sodium floods in, voltage spikes toward plus, and the signal rides down the axon. Heart pacemaker cells do the same trick, and that's what keeps your chest in time. I guess I never really appreciated that the body is basically a self-recharging battery.

The trick with sampling is that most people think it's a software trick, but the craft is in the finding. You're sitting with a crate of records and your ears are hunting for a little melodic fragment that still works when the needle drops. You can spend hours listening, then when you finally hear it, you know in an instant. There's no algorithm for that moment.

Once you have the track, the first job is cleanup. Older recordings carry noise, tape hiss, clicks, and room ambience that has to be pulled out. I do it manually, which is slower but way more surgical than any noise-reduction preset. You zoom in on the waveform and nuke the gaps between notes where you can hear the room. If it's a scratchy vinyl rip, you'll often have to trim a little off the start of phrases so you don't start with a pop or crackle.

The interesting part is making the snippet fit the new composition. You have to time-stretch or pitch-shift the fragment so its tempo and key line up with what you're building. Do this carelessly and the sample will sound out of place, like a stranger in the mix. Do it right, and it stops sounding like a borrowed voice and becomes part of the song. For me, that's where sampling stops being a trick and starts feeling like a conversation with the original artist, which is why I'm not just pasting a cool snippet into a track.

A lot of beginners want the sample to be instantly recognizable, and I get that instinct, but the stronger results often come when you only take the smallest honest piece. One chord, a drum fill, a vocal hum, a bass figure. The less you lift, the more you have to build around it, and the more the original track and the new song start sounding like they belong to each other.

The one rule I keep coming back to: a sample should disappear into the new song, not stand out as a citation.

Your head doesn't hurt because your brain is getting squeezed. It's the vessels and nerves wrapped around your skull and scalp that are doing the screaming, and the pain is mostly a signal that something in that plumbing has gone haywire. When I get one, it usually follows a bad night's sleep or a screen marathon, and starts as a tight band around the temples that builds into a pressure behind the eyes. That's usually the trigeminal nerve getting irritated, with the blood vessels in the head dilating and swelling a bit. I've learned that taking it early matters more than waiting it out. A cold pack and a short nap usually beat another cup of coffee. Treat a headache like a warning light: water, dark room, short rest, and if the pattern changes or it's sudden and severe, don't just push through. The pain is real, but it's not your brain literally cracking.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet actually cost a bit more than I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there’d be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

Spacebar rattles. I hit it with the edge of my thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so “example” becomes “eexample” and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I’m typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I’d have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version, and I've sat through a lot of shows before I could actually gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn was one I finally caught, and honestly? It's mixed, maybe slightly worse than mixed. The circular stage is the smart part. You're basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat the view is decent, which is rare in Vegas. Some of the acts are impressive too. The strength stuff, aerialists, and divers are impressive; those people are athletes, no question. But much of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly; if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats done with more clarity. Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. Is there a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. There's too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more has to be better, so they crammed everything in. Ticket note: if you're staying at the Wynn or Encore, there's a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125, which helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. A few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Don't expect to walk away overwhelmed.

It was about two years ago, we called Rockmount Ranch Wear and ordered two shirts for my dad. They never turned up, because the sales rep screwed up the delivery address: her handwritten “7” got read as a “1,” so 5407 became 5401. The folks living at 5401 took the package to their local UPS store to send it back, then it just vanished and nobody heard from them again. A few weeks went by before we found out. In the middle of the dispute, we put in another order for two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the first two; the owner was the one handling things by then. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong door, but wanted the shirts back before any money back. His take on why it went so sideways was that we hadn’t been friendly enough with the neighbours four doors away. In the end we disputed the original charge with our card company and got the credit through.
